implementation_notes: Python enforces presence, not order: a dataclass with kw_only=True (or a hand-written __init__ using a bare * to make parameters keyword-only) makes every required field a keyword the caller must supply in one call - TypeError at run time, and a static error under mypy/pyright - which removes the staged chain's reason to exist for ordinary data objects. Where a fluent builder is genuinely wanted (scripted setup with side effects, test-data factories), it is written with private attributes and a terminal build() that validates and returns a frozen dataclass; typing the chain with one Protocol per step (each method annotated to return the next Protocol) lets a static checker reject an out-of-order chain, which is the closest Python gets to the compile-time guarantee. For nested/DSL shapes, keyword-only parameters plus a context manager are usually clearer than a staged API.
code_sketch:
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True, kw_only=True)
class DbConfig:
    host: str                    # required: TypeError if omitted
    user: str
    port: int = 5432

cfg = DbConfig(host="db.internal", user="svc")
# DbConfig(user="svc")  -> TypeError: __init__() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'host'
pitfalls: Keyword-only enforcement happens at call time: without a type checker (mypy --strict / pyright) a missing required field is a runtime TypeError on the path that executes.
Frozen dataclasses are shallow - a required field holding a list is still mutable - so __post_init__ must validate contents, not just presence.
A fluent builder accumulating into a dict has no ordering guard: validate in build() and make the builder single-use (clear or freeze it) so a stale build() cannot emit partial state.
